question.text: A newsvendor buys at 2 and sells at 5; demand is 20 or 60, each equally likely. Ordering the mean demand of 40 earns an expected 70. Solving the full stochastic model orders 60 and earns 80. A perfect forecast would earn 120. What is the 80 − 70 = 10?
options: The value of the stochastic solution: what modelling the uncertainty earns over plugging in the average
The expected value of perfect information: what a flawless forecast would be worth
The risk premium: what a cautious planner gives up to avoid the worst case
The profit margin on the extra twenty units the stochastic model orders
question.hint: Two of these quantities are in the numbers given. One of them is 120 − 80 and the other is 80 − 70; work out which is which before answering.

explain.g: Planning for the average is not the same as planning for uncertainty, and here it costs ten. That ten is what the extra modelling effort earns — the reason to build the harder model rather than shrug and use the mean. The forty you could earn from a perfect forecast is a different number, and nobody sells perfect forecasts.
explain.y: VSS = 80 − 70 = 10 is the value of the stochastic solution, the gain of the recourse model over the plug-in-the-mean plan. EVPI = 120 − 80 = 40 is the expected value of perfect information, the gain of clairvoyance over the stochastic model. Both are non-negative by construction, so a positive VSS proves nothing on its own — what matters is whether it justifies the modelling effort. The robust max-min plan is a third answer again: order 20 and guarantee 60 whatever happens.
explain.r: The critical ratio is (price − cost)/price = 3/5 = 0.6, and the critical-fractile rule puts Q* at the 0.6 quantile of demand, which is 60 here; this matches the argmax of expected profit directly. Founded in Dantzig, “Linear Programming under Uncertainty,” Management Science 1, 197–206 (1955), and Beale the same year; reference text Birge & Louveaux, Introduction to Stochastic Programming (Springer, 2nd ed., 2011). Every figure is recomputed in tools/verify_or5_or6.py.
